new_statements.rule_in_words: Uninflected words: stress the final syllable if it is heavy (closed by a consonant, or long vowel), otherwise the penult (final short open syllable). Inflected words: stress the last syllable of the stem (i.e. before the inflectional suffixes), except that the suffixes -yi (object-person focus), -i (nominalizer) and -o'k (repetitive) attract the stress to themselves. Right-edge, quantity-sensitive at the word level with a morphological (stem-final) rule once inflection is added.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the snippets seen. Van Haitsma & Van Haitsma 1976: 79-80 (San José El Paraíso) add that in compound verb stems each stem receives the same intensity, with less intensity on the first syllable of two-syllable stems, and that emphatic stress falls on the syllable that ordinarily receives stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress-carrying suffixes -yi, -i, -o'k override the stem-final rule; footnote 8 (content not visible) is attached to the list of stress-carrying suffixes.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (uninflected vs inflected word); Van Haitsma & Van Haitsma 1976: 4, 79-80 describe a clause accent on the clause nucleus and emphatic stress at phrase/clause level. Assembled verbatim from overlapping Google Books snippets of the same page (line-break hyphens 'un- inflected', 'stress- carrying' rejoined); the printed chapter itself was not opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Hoogshagen 1984 and the 1993 dictionary/grammar describe the Mixe of Santa María Nativitas de Coatlán (distrito de Tehuantepec, 'división sureste'); Van Haitsma & Van Haitsma 1976 describe San José El Paraíso, which Glottolog also files under coat1238 (mco). Glottolog lists 'Isthmus Mixe / Guichicovi Mixe / Lowland Mixe' as alternative names of coat1238, but Guichicovi/Isthmus Mixe (mir) is a separate languoid, isth1238; the Guichicovi stress statements already held by the project (Nordell 1977 rule 1 'Stress Placement'; ILV 2018 Breve diccionario del mixe del Istmo §A.12 'El acento', pp. 141-142, under belong to isth1238, not to this entry. Dieterman 2008 is titled 'Isthmus Mixe' but is cited for Coatlán Mixe by Wikipedia; its variety needs checking before use for either code.

new_statements.quote: The phrase accent occurs on the head word of the phrase or clause nucleus. If the head word has more than one syllable, the accent occurs on the final syllable if the syllable ends in a consonant or in the syllable nuclei V·, V:, V", V', VH. The accent occurs on the penultimate syllable if the final syllable ends in syllable nucleus V. Exceptions to these rules for placement of stress are Spanish loans and a set of verbal suffixes: -ip, -im, -ik, -kiš (all Group II suffixes, see Sect. 4.2.2); the nominalizer -in, the stative clause nucleus marker -it̃ and its alternate forms -id̃i and -igi, and the postclitics ic̃ and ik. The suffixes listed above and the clitics never carry accent.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Hoogshagen 1984 statement (final syllable when closed or with a long/complex nucleus, penult when the final syllable has a short vowel). Adds: the phrase/clause domain of the main accent, the duration/intensity/aspiration correlates, an explicit list of never-accented suffixes and clitics with retraction of the accent to the preceding syllable, the Spanish-loan exception, and notes on compound stems and emphasis. Hoogshagen's stress-carrying suffixes (-yi, -i, -o'k) and Van Haitsma's never-accented suffixes are different morphemes, so the two lists are compatible rather than in conflict.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The authors frame accent as a phrase/clause-level feature (§5.8 opens: 'The major accent pattern is a feature of the phrase and clause. Words carry lesser degrees of stress.'). Within the accented head word the position is determined by the shape of the final syllable: final syllable if it is closed by a consonant or has a complex nucleus (half-long V·, long V:, and the glottalized/aspirated nuclei V", V', VH); penultimate if the final syllable has a plain short V. A closed set of suffixes and clitics (-ip, -im, -ik, -kiš, nominalizer -in, stative -it̃/-id̃i/-igi, postclitics ic̃, ik) never take accent; when one or two of them follow, 'the accent falls on the syllable preceding both nonaccented morphemes' (p. 79). The accented syllable is longer and louder, and word-final voiceless stops are aspirated only there (pp. 12-13, 79).
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 79: 'Words carry lesser degrees of stress.' p. 80: 'Clause accent occurs in the clause nucleus on the verb phrase. Peripheral elements which are words are not accented. Peripheral elements which are phrases and noun phrase specifiers receive a phrase accent. Doublets carry accent on each phrase head, or in the case of clause-nucleus doublets, on each nucleus head.' and 'In compound verb stems, each stem receives the same intensity, with less intensity on the first syllable of two-syllable stems (see Sect. 4.1). The suffix -ta·y "all" is pronounced with less intensity when followed by a stressed suffix.' p. 4: 'A prominent stress occurs on the clause nucleus.. The head of the phrase always carries a phrase stress.'
new_statements.exceptions: p. 79: 'Spanish loans which are not suffixed or incorporated into compound stems are accented on the syllable on which the accent falls when used in Spanish. Spanish loans which are followed by a suffix or incorporated into compound stems follow the rules for Mixe.' (examples p. 80: sábado, miérkoles vs. ganaɾ-áHt). The never-accented suffixes and clitics listed in the quote. p. 80: 'Stress is often used for emphasis. The emphatic stress always occurs on the syllable that ordinarily receives stress, but occurs with greater intensity.'
new_statements.identity_note: Van Haitsma & Van Haitsma 1976 describe the Mixe of San José El Paraíso (their own title); the SIL archive record lists its subject language as Coatlán Mixe [mco], and Dieterman 2008 (fn 58, p. 38) states that the language of San José El Paraíso 'is considered to be the same language as Coatlán Mixe'. Dieterman 2008 itself is about Isthmus Mixe of San Juan Guichicovi (isth1238), not Coatlán Mixe.

sources.citation: Kuznetsova, Natalia. 2025. The rise of ternary quantity and its alignment with laryngeal articulations. Linguistic Typology 29(2): 319–360. doi:10.1515/lingty-2023-0070
sources.quote: Vocalic ternary quantity before stops and sonorants (Table 8-a-c) has been described for the Coatlán (“Cn”), San José El Paraíso (“SJ”), and Camotlán (“Ca”) dialects of Lowland Oaxacan Mixe (Mexico). Lowland Mixe varieties contain six prosodic types of syllabic nuclei in stressed (foot-final) syllables, so it is a MULTIPLE pattern (Table 8-a-d; examples are from Bickford 1985; Dieterman van Haitsma and van Haitsma 1976; Hoogshagen 1959; Wichmann 1995). In paradigms, Q2 alternates with either Q1 or Q3.
